title: The Group as Polarizer
text:
In the early 1960s, researchers found that groups often made riskier decisions after discussion than their members had made alone, which was called the risky shift. Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni in Paris suspected that risk was not the real story.

They worked with French secondary school students. Each student first privately gave their opinion on a series of statements about two topics: General Charles de Gaulle, then president, and Americans. On average, the students were mildly favorable toward de Gaulle and mildly unfavorable toward Americans. Then small groups discussed each statement until they reached agreement, and afterward each student gave a private opinion again.

After discussion, attitudes did not move toward caution or toward risk. They moved further in the direction the group already leaned. Views of de Gaulle became more favorable, and views of Americans became more negative. The group consensus and the later private opinions were both more extreme than the original average.

Moscovici and Zavalloni called this group polarization. The idea explained the earlier risky shift and also the cases in which groups became more cautious: discussion strengthens whatever tendency the members already share.
lesson: Discussing with like-minded people tends to push everyone further the same way. Before trusting a group's strong conclusion, check where its members started.
source: Moscovici, S., and Zavalloni, M. (1969). The group as a polarizer of attitudes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 12(2), 125-135.
